analysis.one_liner: Lets bankruptcy judges cut mortgage interest and rewrite loan terms for homeowners facing foreclosure.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in November 2010 with six weeks left in the Congress, drew zero cosponsors, was never voted on, and died in committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let homeowners in Chapter 13 bankruptcy change the terms of a mortgage on the home they live in, when that home is already in foreclosure. Bankruptcy courts could freeze an adjustable interest rate, replace it with a fixed market rate plus a risk premium, and require payments to go directly to the lender. It would also stop lenders from getting courts to lift bankruptcy protection so they could foreclose, and it would skip the credit-counseling requirement for people facing foreclosure. In exchange, homeowners who later sold the house for a profit would owe the lender 30% of the capital gains.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners who file for Chapter 13 bankruptcy while facing foreclosure on their primary residence. They could keep their homes by having a bankruptcy judge reset the loan to a fixed, market-rate interest and restructure payments, instead of losing the house to foreclosure. The bill also shields their bankruptcy case from being lifted so a lender can foreclose during the case.

how_it_helps.text: Lets a Chapter 13 bankruptcy plan modify a mortgage on the debtor's primary residence when foreclosure has been noticed — freezing adjustable rates and setting fixed interest at the published market average prime offer rate plus a reasonable risk premium.

Excludes foreclosures of the debtor's principal residence from the rule that bankruptcy courts must lift the automatic stay 'for cause', so lenders could not get court permission to foreclose during the case on that ground.
Waives the bankruptcy credit-counseling requirement for a debtor whose home is the subject of a foreclosure notice, removing a step that could otherwise delay or block the filing.
Extends the deadline to file a Chapter 13 plan from 14 to 30 days when the plan modifies a mortgage, giving filers more time to prepare it.
Requires the homeowner to certify under penalty of perjury that they already asked the lender to modify the loan before filing, keeping bankruptcy as a last step rather than a first one.

analysis.who_pays: Mortgage lenders and investors. Loans written before enactment could have their interest rates reset below the contract rate and their terms rewritten by a judge, reducing the amounts lenders and mortgage-backed investors recover. Homeowners who sell at a profit within ten years of the plan must pay the lender 30% of the capital gains, which claws back part of the relief.

drawbacks.text: Homeowners must share the upside: if they sell the home for a gain within ten years of the plan, 30% of the capital gains goes back to the lender.
The changes apply retroactively to bankruptcy cases already open when the bill takes effect, not just future filings.
Loans guaranteed by FHA, VA, or USDA are expressly left unchanged, so the protection would not reach a large share of mortgage borrowers.

Lenders have long argued that letting judges reduce mortgage balances and rates raises the risk on all home loans and could push up rates for future borrowers — this was the core industry objection to mortgage 'cramdown' proposals; this bill limits that exposure by requiring a risk premium, a fixed market-rate benchmark, and the ten-year profit-sharing condition, but it does not eliminate it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the targeted group — homeowners in foreclosure who file bankruptcy — the benefit is large: keeping a home instead of losing it. The costs fall on lenders and investors holding the affected loans, spread widely, and the bill's own conditions (market-rate benchmark, risk premium, profit-sharing) make the relief less generous than a straight principal write-down. The main honest objection is that shifting losses onto mortgage investors could raise borrowing costs at the margin for everyone else buying a home.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with six weeks left in the Congress, sent to the Judiciary Committee and then a subcommittee, and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim McDermott introduced the bill on November 18, 2010, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the same day.
On December 20, 2010, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Commercial and Administrative Law — no further action followed.
No member of either party signed on as a cosponsor.
The bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote, and the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, killing it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage lenders and investors came out ahead. Because the bill died, they keep their full contractual right to foreclose on primary residences and no bankruptcy judge can reset the interest rates or terms of their loans. Homeowners facing foreclosure received no new protection.

for.name: Rep. Jim McDermott
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made introductory remarks; it had no cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on the Judiciary leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill was passed to a subcommittee on December 20, 2010 and stayed there until the Congress ended.

against.name: House Financial Services lending and servicing interests
against.what_they_did: Opposed similar bankruptcy mortgage-modification ('cramdown') legislation during the 2009-2010 foreclosure crisis, arguing it would raise mortgage rates; their position shaped why such bills repeatedly stalled in the House and Senate.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no other member cosponsored — not even from the 253-member Democratic majority — so the record shows no measurable support from either party.

industries.note: The bill lets a bankruptcy judge freeze adjustable rates and rewrite terms of mortgages facing foreclosure on primary homes, and blocks lenders from getting the bankruptcy stay lifted to foreclose. Lenders lose some contractual leverage and expected recoveries; for homeowners that same leverage is what the bill takes away.
Resetting loan terms below contract rates reduces cash flows on securitized loans. The bill's risk premium and 30% profit-sharing condition soften but do not eliminate the loss.

industries.industry: Federal housing guaranty programs (FHA, VA, USDA)
industries.note: The bill explicitly leaves government-guaranteed loan obligations unchanged, so federal guarantee exposure is preserved even as private mortgages are modified.
